idiom_name: int64_t minor units plus a currency struct (exponent carried as data)
implementation_notes: C offers neither a decimal type nor currency data, so the pattern survives as a discipline around int64_t: store the amount as a count of the currency's minor unit, carry the ISO 4217 code and the exponent in the same struct, and route every operation through functions (money_add, money_sub, money_scale) that refuse mismatched currencies. That replaces the classic Money class with a small value struct plus free functions; rounding is hand-written integer arithmetic such as floor division with a tie correction, and the scale is data rather than a literal 100. The struct and the naming discipline are justified precisely because the compiler enforces nothing: the alternative is not a class but scattered int64 variables whose unit lives in comments. Where sub-minor precision is unavoidable, link a decimal library such as decNumber or GMP instead of reintroducing double.
pitfalls: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C: an int64_t total can wrap or be optimised away, so additions must be range-checked (or widened) before they happen.
Integer division truncates toward zero rather than toward negative infinity, so a naive largest-remainder allocator distributes the leftover minor units wrongly for negative amounts.
Carrying the scale in the struct is the only way to keep JPY (no minor unit) and BHD (three decimals) honest; a hard-coded 100 converts both wrongly.
strcmp-based currency equality is case- and whitespace-sensitive, so the three-letter code has to be normalised at construction.
